food.text: In 1937 the Koryo-saram, ethnic Koreans of the former Soviet Union, were deported to Central Asia, where 171,781 people were removed by 25 October. The money the government promised them never came, and most of the deportees were rice farmers and fishermen who struggled in the arid climate. Estimates suggest 40,000 of them died in 1937 and 1938 for these reasons. Their cuisine has since become popular throughout the former Soviet Union, and the dish morkovcha, a kimchi variant made with carrots, is now widely available in grocery stores there.

A typical Central Asian meal begins with tea or fresh tandyr nan bread, followed by soup or pulled noodles. The main course is often a pilov of meat, rice and carrots. Hundreds of variations are possible, using herbs, dried fruits like raisins and apricots, and nuts.
Potatoes were introduced to Uzbekistan by the Soviets. Some elder Uzbeks still refuse to eat them, even though the cuisine is otherwise built on bread, noodles and rice.

In 1953, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev launched the Virgin Lands campaign, sending hundreds of thousands of young volunteers to farm the steppe of northern Kazakhstan and southern Siberia. During the summer of 1954 alone, 300,000 Komsomol volunteers took part.

Tea is the most popular beverage in Central Asia. Green tea with cream is more common in Kyrgyz cuisine, while black tea is more common in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. People gather to socialize over tea in a teahouse called a chaikhana.

A nomadic diet based on meat and dairy products is found in Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Besh barmak, a lamb dish eaten with the hands, and horse meat are found only in some regions, mostly Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.

Uzbekistan's oldest and most famous winery is the Khovrenko Winery in Samarkand, established in 1927. The country has 14 wineries in all. Uzbek wines have received international awards and are exported to Russia and other countries in Central Asia.
The Samarkand Winery produces a range of dessert wines from local grape varieties: Gulyakandoz, Shirin, Aleatiko, and Kabernet likernoe. The last name is literally Cabernet dessert wine in Russian.

In Uzbekistan, green tea called kok choy is the most popular and is typically served unsweetened in small ceramic piyola bowls. It is drunk with dishes such as plov or shashlik. For festive occasions there is shirchoy, a salty milk tea prepared with butter that reflects the region's steppe heritage.

In Central Asia, the Dungan people, descendants of the Hui, operate restaurants serving Chinese Islamic cuisine. Unlike much of the region's food, it is eaten with chopsticks. The cuisine uses wheat noodles as its staple, rather than rice.

Although the Virgin Lands campaign initially boosted Soviet grain output, intensive cultivation of Kazakhstan's steppe caused significant soil erosion, turning the project into a long-term environmental disaster. Even so, wheat sown there in 1998 still covered almost twice the area farmed in 1953.

Fermented drinks tied to pastoral traditions remain common in Uzbek cuisine, including qatiq and kumis, which is fermented mare's milk. Ayran, a cold, salted yogurt drink, is also popular, as is chalop, a chilled mixture of yogurt, dill, cilantro and vegetables that works as both a beverage and a light dish.

art.text: Mongol zurag is a style of painting developed in the early 20th century. It shows secular, nationalist themes in mineral paint on cotton, a medium similar to Tibetan thangka. This set it apart from both traditional Buddhist fine art and the socialist realism favoured during the Mongolian People's Republic.

Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan, holds the world record for the highest density of white marble-clad buildings, with 48,589,619 square feet of marble. The article links this to the country's large gas reserves.

The first years of the Soviet regime in Central Asia saw the appearance of modernism, which took inspiration from the Russian avant-garde movement. Until the 1980s, Central Asian arts developed along with the general tendencies of Soviet arts.

Ten modernist buildings and urban complexes built in Tashkent between the 1960s and 1990s were designated a World Heritage Site in 2026. The site is called "Tashkent Modernist Architecture. Modernity and Tradition in Central Asia".
Balduugiin Sharav pioneered zurag painting in the aftermath of the 1921 Revolution. His work One Day in Mongolia remains one of the most celebrated works of Mongolian art.
Dushanbe was known as Stalinabad from 1931 to 1961. Its Palace of Nations, built in 2002, has in front of it a 165-metre flagpole that was once the tallest in the world.

Zurag paintings of everyday life, set on collective farms or in traditional pastoral nomadic scenes, became popular in the 1950s and 1960s. This followed the success of Ürjingiin Yadamsüren's The Old Fiddler.

Under the state, overtly religious themes in zurag were discouraged, though historical depictions of the 1921 Revolution and earlier national figures were popular. Since democracy was established in 1992, interest in the style has resurged, with scenes from the Secret History of the Mongols and the life of Genghis Khan.

Dushanbe's National Library of Tajikistan, officially opened in 2012, is the largest library in Central Asia and was built to look like an open book. The nearby National Museum of Tajikistan opened in 2011 with 22 exhibition spaces.
Ashgabat's Monument of Neutrality was completed in 1998 to commemorate the president at the time, Saparmurat Niyazov. The structure represents Turkmenistan's international neutrality.
Recent zurag paintings have included overtly religious imagery inspired by pre-Buddhist shamanism. They have also become more symbolic and less strictly representational.

Ashgabat International Airport terminal opened in 2016 at a cost of $2.3 billion. In the city, the Wedding Palace features a Turkmen star encapsulating an Earth that displays the country of Turkmenistan.

war.text: In 1916 discontent in Russian Turkestan boiled over in the Basmachi Revolt, sparked by a decree conscripting the native population into labour battalions. They had previously been exempt from military service. Thousands of settlers were killed, and this was matched by Russian reprisals, particularly against the nomadic population.

During the Soviet–Japanese War of 1945, known in Mongolia as the Liberation War of 1945, the Mongolian army advanced to the Great Wall of China. Manchukuo, a puppet state of the Empire of Japan, had earlier invaded Barga and part of Inner Mongolia with Japanese help.

In 1943 Stalin deported all Kalmyks to Siberia. Around half of the 97,000–98,000 deported died before being allowed to return home in 1957, and the Soviet government forbade teaching the Kalmyk language during the deportation.

During the Central Asian Revolt of 1916, Kazakhs attacked Russian and Cossack villages, killing indiscriminately, and the Russians' revenge was merciless. A military force drove 300,000 Kazakhs to flee into the mountains or to China. When approximately 80,000 of them returned the next year, many were slaughtered by Tsarist forces.

Early in 1918, the Bolsheviks of the Tashkent Soviet launched an attack on the autonomous Jadid government in Kokand, which left 14,000 dead. The Tashkent Soviet was made up entirely of Russian soldiers and railway workers, with no Muslim members.
Japan forced Inner Mongolian and Barga people to fight against the Mongolians. Instead, they surrendered to the Mongolians and started to fight against their Japanese and Manchu allies.

The Tajik Civil War broke out in 1992 between the Tajik government and a coalition of opponents led by a radical Islamist group, the Islamic Renaissance Party. It lasted until 1997, and over 50,000 people were killed out of a population of 6 million, while another 250,000 fled the country to Afghanistan, Uzbekistan or elsewhere. The war showed other former Soviet republics, already wary of Islam in politics, the dangers of Islamic opposition groups.
Local resistance to the Bolsheviks in Central Asia continued well into the 1920s. Soviet historians dismissed the fighters as 'Basmachi' or 'Banditry'.

During the war, Marshal Khorloogiin Choibalsan called on Inner Mongolians and Xinjiang Oirats to migrate to Mongolia, but the Soviet Army blocked the Inner Mongolian migrants' way. Only a few arrived, including about 800 Uzemchins.

Japan-backed Inner Mongolian leaders founded the Inner Mongolian Army in 1929, and the nominally independent Mengjiang state was established with Japanese support in 1936. The Inner Mongolian Army disbanded after the end of World War II.

During the deportation, many Kalmyks joined the German Army. Under the Law of the Russian Federation of April 26, 1991, repressions against Kalmyks and other peoples were qualified as acts of genocide.

literature.text: Uzbek literature was originally written in three main scripts: Arabic, Latin, and Cyrillic. In 1933, the government of Uzbekistan introduced a modified version of the Latin alphabet.

Uzbek literature was influenced by Russian and Turkish literature. The Russian conquest of Central Asia had a significant impact on it, and that mark continued until the Soviet Union was dissolved in 1991.

In 1945, Mongolia began composing and selecting poems for a new national anthem. The Arts Department issued rules for a closed poetry competition with a deadline of 31 December 1945, but works kept being submitted until April 1946.

The writer Tsendiin Damdinsüren took part in the poetry competition for Mongolia's new anthem and wrote its lyrics. Marshal Khorloogiin Choibalsan personally took part in the selection, listening to many versions of the melody and song.

Established in 1943 and headquartered in Tashkent, SADUM was charged with publishing spiritual materials under strict state control. It supported several printings of the Qur'an, the first of which appeared in 1957.
literature.source_title: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan

literature.text: Uzbek literature treats the Chagatai language as an important reference point. Chagatai was one of the most widely accessible languages in the region from the 14th to the 20th century, and modern Uzbek has its roots in it.

Between 1924 and 1950, Mongolia's anthem was the "Mongol Internationale", with lyrics by Sonombaljiriin Buyannemekh. It is often wrongly listed as the Mongolian version of "The Internationale", though the two songs have almost nothing in common apart from similar titles.

In 1961, in line with the 1960 constitution, Tsevegmidin Gaitav and Choijilin Chimed changed the anthem's words. The new lyrics referred to the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party and dropped references to Soviet and Mongolian leaders. The original lyrics were restored in early 1991.

Since 1991, most of the 1950 anthem lyrics have been in use again, but the second verse praising Lenin, Stalin, Sükhbaatar and Choibalsan was removed. On 6 July 2006, the Mongolian Parliament revised the lyrics to commemorate Genghis Khan.

In 2006, in anticipation of the 800th anniversary of the Mongol Empire, six writers were mobilized to partly change the anthem's text. The revision was meant to reflect a new state that had escaped foreign oppression, rather than the country's rich heritage and history.

SADUM's Qur'an printings were not all alike. From 1969 and 1970, a version was published that was based on a local 1913 Qur'an written in the naskh script. It followed the 1960 printing, which was based on an Egyptian model.
literature.source_title: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan

science.text: On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the world's first man-made satellite, from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in the Kazakh Steppe. The cosmodrome, founded in 1955, became the chief base of the Soviet space program.
On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin launched aboard Vostok 1 from Baikonur, becoming the first human in space. The launch pad he used was later renamed Gagarin's Start in his honor.

Construction of the Nurek Dam on Tajikistan's Vakhsh River began in 1961 and finished in 1980, making it briefly the tallest dam in the world at 304 meters. Built by the Soviet Union, it remains the second tallest dam ever constructed.

The Aral Sea, once the world's third largest lake at 68,000 square kilometers, began shrinking in the 1960s after Soviet irrigation projects diverted the rivers that fed it. By 2007 it had shrunk to 10 percent of its original size, splitting into four lakes. The dying sea left plains of salt and toxic chemicals whose wind-borne dust poisoned the people living there: high rates of certain cancers, respiratory illnesses including mostly drug-resistant tuberculosis, and anaemia, with child mortality at 75 per 1,000 in 2009 and maternal mortality at 12 in every 1,000.
In 1963, Valentina Tereshkova launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome to become the first woman in space. Her flight followed Yuri Gagarin's historic 1961 mission from the same launch site.

The Nurek Dam's power station houses nine hydroelectric generating units and, as of early 2024, supplies 70 percent of Tajikistan's electricity. About 5,000 people were resettled from the area flooded by its reservoir.

To save the shrinking North Aral Sea, Kazakhstan completed the Dike Kokaral dam in 2005. By 2008 the water level there had risen 12 meters to 42 meters, and by 2013 salinity had dropped enough for fishing to resume.

In October 2024, Kazakhstan held a referendum on building its first nuclear power plant, leveraging its position as the world's largest uranium producer. Voters approved the plan, and the plant is set to be built in the village of Ulken near Lake Balkhash.

In 1960, a prototype R-16 intercontinental ballistic missile exploded before launch at Baikonur Cosmodrome, killing more than 100 people. The same steppe launch site had, just three years earlier, sent Sputnik 1 into orbit.

In 2004, Russia and Kazakhstan agreed to jointly build the Baiterek launch complex at Baikonur for Russia's Angara rocket, each holding a 50 percent stake. Unlike older boosters, the Angara burns kerosene and oxygen, which are less hazardous to the environment than the toxic fuels used previously.

politics.text: In 1991, the Soviet Union ended and the five modern Central Asian nations became independent. They are Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. The Russian sphere of influence had remained in the region until then, even after the Russian Empire collapsed during World War I.
In 1924, Mongolia became a communist People's Republic. It was swept up by the Russian Revolution, yet it never became a Soviet republic.

Borjigin nobles proclaimed Mongolia's independence in 1911 and established the Bogd Khanate. The Borjigin held power over Mongolia for many centuries, even under the Qing, and lost it only when Communists took control in the 20th century.

In 1916, the Russians removed the Muslim exemption from conscription during the First World War, sparking the Central Asian Revolt of 1916. After the Russian Revolution of 1917, a Jadid government met in Kokand and declared Turkestan's autonomy, but the forces of the Tashkent Soviet quickly crushed it.

The Soviets redrew Central Asia's map in stages. In 1924 they created the Uzbek SSR and the Turkmen SSR, and in 1929 the Tajik SSR was split from the Uzbek SSR. The Kyrgyz Autonomous Oblast became an SSR in 1936.

The Bolsheviks created a new political elite favorable towards Marxist ideology, using propaganda and appointing officials who backed their policies. This happened during the division of Central Asia into separate republics along ethnic lines in the 1920s and 1930s.

Guerrillas known as Basmachi kept fighting the communists in Central Asia until 1924. The main independence forces had been rapidly crushed, and the semi-autonomous states of Bukhara and Khiva were also invaded.

In 1926, the Soviet government decided it had consolidated control over Central Asia sufficiently to shift official policy from toleration of Islam to condemnation. Between 1927 and 1929, the state ran a campaign to shut down mosques. The operation was not well documented, but existing accounts indicate it was often violent and poorly controlled, often carried out by self-appointed officials who arrested imams and destroyed buildings, denouncing Islam as an enemy of communism.

Navaanneren Setsen Khan, the last ruling Chinggisid and Borjigin aristocrat holding princely and monarchical status, was executed in 1937. Joseph Stalin's associates had some 30,000 Mongols executed, Borjigin nobles among them, in a series of campaigns against Mongol culture and religion. Aristocratic descent was something to be forgotten in the socialist period.

The Taliban's takeover of Afghanistan in 1996 further emphasized to the governments of the Central Asian republics the threat of Islamic opposition groups. These governments were already wary after the Tajik Civil War, which began in 1992 and lasted until 1997. In it, over 50,000 people were killed out of a population of 6 million, and another 250,000 fled the country to Afghanistan, Uzbekistan or elsewhere.

Anandyn Amar, a member of the People's Great Khural, a former prime minister and one of the many communist Borjigin Mongols who founded the Mongolian People's Republic, was executed by the government in 1941. The article says he was killed as a result of internal Mongolian class struggle. The communist state he helped found thus put to death one of its own founders.

The communist regime banned the use of Mongolian clan names in the 1920s. When the ban was lifted in 1997 and people were told they had to have surnames, some families had lost knowledge of their clan association. Around 700,000 people are now registered under the family name Borjigin in Mongolia.

philosophy.text: The Russian Empire broadly tolerated Islam during its rule over Central Asia from the mid-1860s to 1917. The Russian Revolutions of 1917 and the civil war that followed brought Soviet rule, and with it Marxist opposition to religion.

In 1926 the Soviet government decided it had consolidated control over Central Asia sufficiently to shift official policy from toleration of Islam to condemnation. Private religious schools were closed in favor of state-run public ones. Between 1927 and 1929 the state ran a campaign to shut down mosques that, according to existing accounts, was often violent and poorly controlled. It was often carried out by self-appointed officials who arrested imams and destroyed buildings, denouncing Islam as an enemy of communism.

In April 1932, Buddhist monks in Western Mongolia led an armed uprising against the government's radical policies, which had confiscated hundreds of feudal and clergy estates, taxed the church heavily, forbidden it to teach children and barred it from recruiting new monks. The revolt is locally known as "The Shambhala War." Some leaders sought military help from the 9th Panchen Lama, who was locked in Lhasa, and in October 1932 the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Army, with Soviet assistance, fully crushed the uprising.

After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, Tengrism, a form of Central Asian shamanism centered on the sky god Tengri, experienced a revival. In Kyrgyzstan, an ideological committee chaired by Dastan Sarygulov suggested it as a pan-Turkic national ideology after the 2005 presidential elections.

Shiism is practiced in Central Asia in two distinct forms. Ismailis predominate on the Pamir plateau and in the western Tian Shan mountains, while Imamis form a large minority in the Zarafshan river valley, from Samarkand to Bukhara.

Persecution of Buddhism in Mongolia peaked during the Great Repression of 1937 to 1939, when Khorloogiin Choibalsan orchestrated the purge of political opponents and religious and minority populations. In 1938, amid accusations that the church and monasteries were trying to cooperate with the Japanese, the remaining monasteries were dissolved, their property seized, and their monks secularized, interned or executed. Monastic buildings that had not been destroyed were turned into government offices or schools. An estimated 20,000 to 35,000 "enemies of the revolution" were executed, three to five percent of Mongolia's population, and Robert Rupen reports over 112,000 monks in the 1920s, yet by the 1940s nearly every monk was either dead or had apostatized.

The Jadids were a Muslim modernist movement who argued that Muslim peoples in Tsarist Russia had fallen into moral and societal decay. They believed this could be cured only by a new kind of knowledge and European-modeled cultural reform. They championed the Usul-i Jadid, or "new method," of teaching, from which their name derives.

The 9th Jebtsundamba Khutughtu was recognized in 1936 as a reincarnation of the Bogd Khan, third highest lama in Tibetan Buddhism. The Dalai Lama kept his identity secret until 1990 because the Communist Mongolian People's Republic persecuted Buddhism. When the 14th Dalai Lama escaped from Tibet in 1959, he fled too, fearing his identity would be revealed and he would be killed or used by the Communists for propaganda. He did not live in Mongolia until the final year of his life.

In the early 1920s the Bolsheviks cooperated with the Jadids, Muslims working towards social and cultural reforms such as improved education. The partnership helped the Bolsheviks accomplish their goals before Soviet policy turned against Islam.

After the October Revolution of 1917, the Jadids resumed language reform and new-method teaching with renewed fervor. By the early 1920s they felt comfortable allying with the Bolsheviks, and large numbers of Jadids joined the Communist Party to gain the benefits of Soviet rule.

The 9th Jebtsundamba Khutughtu was enthroned at Gandantegchinlen Monastery in Ulaanbaatar in July 1999 while visiting Mongolia on a tourist visa. In November 2011 he was enthroned as head of Mongolia's Buddhists. In 2016 the Dalai Lama said he believed the 10th Khutughtu had been reborn in Mongolia, and the boy was anointed in 2023.

The term "yellow shamanism" was introduced in 1992 by Sendenjav Dulam. It names a Mongolian and Siberian shamanism that incorporates Buddhist rituals, "yellow" referring to the Yellow sect of Tibetan Buddhism. Otgony Pürev argues that yellow shamanism has by now ceased to exist anywhere.

Among the Buryats near Lake Baikal, a nineteenth-century division held that black shamanism called on evil deities to bring people misfortune, while white shamanism invoked good deities for happiness and prosperity. By the twentieth century this had completely changed. Today black shamanism invokes traditional shamanic deities, while white shamanism invokes Buddhist deities and recites Buddhist incantations but wears black shamanist accoutrements.

Shamanism stayed alive among the isolated Nganasan people of northern Siberia into the twentieth century. In 1931, A. Popov observed the shaman Dyukhade Kosterkin imitating a polar bear, and he was believed to have transformed into one. The last notable Nganasan shaman's seances were filmed in the 1970s.

culture.text: Islam has been practiced in Central Asia since the beginning of Islamic history, and the Sunni branch is the most widely practiced religion there. In the 20th century, the Soviet Union in Soviet Central Asia and the People's Republic of China in Xinjiang enacted severe restrictions on religious practice. In Soviet Central Asia this included a 1927 to 1929 campaign that shut down mosques, often violently, with imams arrested and buildings destroyed.

Non-Muslim areas of Greater Central Asia, such as Mongolia, still share a common religious heritage with neighboring areas through elements such as Tengrism. The region was historically interconnected religiously, economically and otherwise.

Mongolian is the official national language of Mongolia, spoken by nearly 2.8 million people according to a 2010 estimate. It is also the official provincial language of China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, where there are at least 4.1 million ethnic Mongols.

In 1926, the Soviet government decided it had consolidated control over Central Asia and shifted its official policy from toleration of Islam to condemnation. It closed private religious schools in favor of state-run public ones.

The Mongolian language in Inner Mongolia has moved through cycles. It declined in the late Qing period, revived between 1947 and 1965, declined again from 1966 to 1976, revived from 1977 to 1992, and declined a third time between 1995 and 2012.

Although the Soviet Union supported the Mongolian People's Republic, it carried out political, economic and cultural policies against Mongolia until its fall in 1991. The aim was to prevent pan-Mongolism and other irredentist movements.

Southern Khalkha Mongols now living in Inner Mongolia are believed to have been moved south from the Khangai Mountains. Every new lunar year they perform special Khangai Mountain worshipping ceremonies, facing northwest and praying. No other Southern Mongols have such rituals.

Between 1927 and 1929, the Soviet state ran a campaign to shut down mosques in Central Asia. The operation was not well documented, but existing accounts indicate it was often violent and poorly controlled. It was often carried out by self-appointed officials who arrested imams and destroyed buildings, denouncing Islam as an enemy of communism.

During the first few years of Bolshevik rule in the early 1920s, Soviet officials took a pragmatic approach to religion. They prioritized modernizing culture, building schools and improving the position of women, and cooperated with the Jadids, Muslims working towards social and cultural reforms such as improved education.

In 1919, a Conciliatory Commission for Turkestan Affairs was established to try to improve relations between the locals and the Communists. New policies were introduced that respected local customs and religion.
From 1964 to 1991, the city of Aktau was named "Shevchenko" in honour of the Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko (1814–1861). He had been assigned to the area on military work.

Some Mongols in China, such as the Tumets, may have completely or partially lost the ability to speak their language. They are still registered as ethnic Mongols and identify as such, as do the children of inter-ethnic Mongol-Chinese marriages.
